extracted.intended_audience: patent scholars, patent prosecutors, USPTO policymakers, patent litigators
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating interpretive rules for patent claim construction (broadest reasonable construction vs. PHOSITA) and their effects on public notice, prosecution, and litigation. Focuses on how rules influence prior art searching, claim drafting incentives, prosecution records, and the outer bounds of claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory definiteness (35 U.S.C. § 112)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must satisfy the statutory requirement that claims be definite (35 U.S.C. § 112).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO should not avoid the responsibility of ensuring definiteness by delegating it to another party; doing so is contrary to the original purpose of the broadest reasonable construction rule — to enhance public notice at the time of a patent grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest reasonable construction (BRC) rule (as applied by USPTO)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the BRC rule, the USPTO applies the broadest reasonable construction of claim terms during prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended to enhance public notice at grant by construing claims broadly during examination; in practice, lack of consensus about how to apply BRC (e.g., whether examiners use dictionaries) produces examiner-dependent variability, reduces ex ante incentives for precise drafting, affects scope of prior art searches, and does not reliably define the outer limits of claim scope for later litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: PHOSITA rule for prosecution and reexamination
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should be interpreted as a person having ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA) would have understood them at the filing date in light of the specification and prosecution history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dictionary definitions implying broader interpretations should yield to meanings made clear by the specification. Adopting the PHOSITA rule in the USPTO aims to improve certainty in claim construction, reduce costs from conflicting rules used by courts vs. USPTO, and make the prosecution record more useful to later courts and litigants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enhancing public notice — iterative improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: One method public notice is enhanced is through iterative improvements: prosecution (examiner prior-art searches and rejections) iteratively narrows and clarifies claim scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BRC and PHOSITA affect iterative improvements differently: BRC encourages broader prior-art searches (revealing more art), but its interpretive variability limits predictability; PHOSITA may cause examiners to scrutinize specification and issue more rejections for vagueness but may reduce the scope of prior-art considered (possibly lowering some obviousness rejections). The public record under PHOSITA is likely more useful to courts because it reflects ordinary-meaning discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enhancing public notice — ex ante incentives for precise claiming
rubrics_metrics.description: A rule should encourage applicants, before filing, to draft claims precisely (ex ante incentives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BRC does not necessarily create ex ante incentives because applicants do not know how examiners will apply the rule; applicants also face other barriers (drafting skill, funds, perceived patent value). PHOSITA may not materially change these incentives either; patentees who desire vagueness will still often draft broadly because of costs and strategic considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enhancing public notice — defining outer limits of claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A rule should help define the outer bounds of claim scope so third parties can understand legal reach of a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neither BRC nor PHOSITA guarantees that the examiner can set the outer limits at prosecution because (1) examiners rarely disclose their constructions in the public record, and (2) courts do not give examiner interpretations binding deference and may construe claims differently at litigation. Thus, adoption of PHOSITA alone will not necessarily prevent unexpected broad constructions in litigation, though PHOSITA-based prosecution histories may be more relevant to courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of specification over dictionary definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification is a key interpretive guide and should take precedence over broad dictionary definitions when the specification indicates a narrower meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phillips supports reliance on the specification to inform claim meaning; dictionary definitions that imply broader interpretations should not be used if the specification makes a narrower meaning clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art search scope tied to claim interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The breadth of the examiner's prior art search should be determined by how the claims are interpreted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under BRC a broad claim construction leads to broader searches (beneficial for revealing art and shaping claims); PHOSITA would likely reduce the scope of prior art searched because claims are construed with ordinary meaning and specification context. The article notes that broad searches could be achieved by separate procedures rather than by interpretive rule alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of examiner's claim interpretation in prosecution record
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should disclose how they construe claim terms in the prosecution history to aid public notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice examiners often do not record their informal assumptions, and examiners almost never testify; absent disclosure, the prosecution history will not reveal the examiner's view and courts cannot rely on it. Enhancing disclosure would make the prosecution record more useful to courts and third parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid delegation/blind reliance on others for claim definiteness
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO should not avoid its responsibility to ensure definite claims by delegating that responsibility to other parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delegation undermines the purpose of the BRC rule to enhance public notice at the time of patent grant; the agency must retain responsibility for claim definiteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity of claim meaning across prosecution and litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim meaning should not vary with time or audience; courts and the USPTO should use consistent interpretive standards to avoid a 'zone of uncertainty.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflicting standards impose costs on patentees and third parties. A single rule (e.g., PHOSITA applied both in prosecution and litigation) would reduce costs and improve predictability of claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court non-deference to USPTO interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal courts do not give automatic deference to the USPTO's understanding of claim terms at any stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when the examiner discloses an interpretation, courts may construe claims differently (sometimes broader), so examiner interpretations cannot be presumed to define the outer bounds of claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims given meaning as of the filing date
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are to be given their meaning as of the date of filing because patent claims are usually written at approximately the time of their filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using a fixed reference date (filing date) for claim meaning promotes ascertainability and connection to the examiner's understanding at prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical incentives and barriers affecting claim precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical barriers (limited funds, drafting skill, perceived patent value, and applicants' practice of waiting for examiner prior-art search results) affect applicants' willingness and ability to draft precise initial claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These incentives are largely independent of the interpretive rule; applicants often await examiner searches and may rely on iterative amendment rather than investing in exhaustive initial drafting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminate harms of conflicting rules (policy criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A desirable interpretive regime should eliminate harms from using different rules in prosecution and litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different interpretive standards create wasted time, energy, and money and a zone of uncertainty; changing the USPTO rule to align with courts (PHOSITA) is justified to reduce these harms even if net substantive benefits are uncertain.
